items.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002
items.q: I guess I’m thinking of the Ken Burns thing

ctx.x: We were pretty avid fans. I mean yeah, I can believe that. Yeah, I would argue that whatever Bird did was cool. He was, right, I didn’t like him destroying himself. I got to know him quite well. I mean I wanted to be around Bird so much I married his piano player. How’s that? Not really but, no, nobody could say anything about Bird. He was our God you know, a musical God.

When I watch some films, I guess I’m thinking of the Ken Burns thing, a lot of times they make assumptions. I think they’re assumptions, about the social implications of some of the jazz pioneers, as if his music was a social statement about freeing himself, freeing the
members of his race. Do you think that what he did had social implications or was it more just his musical prowess?
